title: Manage AI Model Lifecycle and Security Governance
intro: How individual models are governed from approval to retirement: named ownership, risk tiers and approval workflows; model cards and approved model registries; securing the deployment pipeline; sanitising inputs and outputs, releasing updates and rolling back; monitoring drift, bias and anomalies in production; and keeping audit trails of AI data events that protect privacy.
objectives: Assign model ownership, classify models by risk, and design approval workflows proportionate to each tier
Document models with model cards, and use an approved registry as an enforceable deployment control
Secure the deployment pipeline: validation gates, safe packaging, signing, hardened serving and pipeline credentials
Sanitise model inputs and outputs, and release and roll back model updates safely
Monitor models for drift, bias and security anomalies, and feed the results back into governance
Design audit trails for AI data events that support investigations and compliance while protecting privacy

sections.title: Model governance: ownership, risk tiers and approvals

scenes.title: Who owns this model?
scenes.sub: Ownership, risk classification and approval workflows
scenes.say: Every model in production should have a named owner, a risk classification and an approval record. Without them, nobody is accountable when a model fails. | This video covers model governance: who owns models, how they are classified by risk, and how approval workflows scale with that risk.

scenes.title: Roles in model governance
scenes.say: Model governance assigns clear roles. | The model owner, usually in the business, is accountable for the model’s use and outcomes. | Developers build, document and test it. | Independent validators challenge it before approval: people who didn’t build it, with the authority to insist on changes. | Risk and compliance functions set standards and oversee, as the second line. | And internal audit provides independent assurance, as the third line.

scenes.title: Risk tiers drive requirements
scenes.say: Risk tiers make governance proportionate. | For example, a tier one model might be an internal drafting aid; tier two, a customer-facing chatbot; tier three, a model that informs credit or hiring decisions. | Validation scales with the tier: self-assessed tests for tier one, peer review and a standard test suite for tier two, and independent validation for tier three. | So does the approver: a product owner, an AI governance lead, or a committee or designated senior owner. | And so does review frequency: perhaps every two years, annually, or every six months and whenever the model changes.

scenes.title: Approving a high-risk model
scenes.say: Here is an approval workflow for a high-risk model. It starts when the use case is proposed, added to the inventory and assigned a risk tier. | The design and the data are approved: purpose, lawful basis, data sources and owners. | Independent validators test performance, robustness and fairness against the requirements. | Security and privacy reviews check threats, controls and impact assessments. | The approver signs off, often with conditions, such as limits on use or extra monitoring. | Then the model is deployed with its monitoring plan, and returns for review on a schedule and on any significant change.

items: Every model has a named, accountable owner
Independent validation provides effective challenge
Risk tiers set validation depth, approver and review frequency
Approvals carry conditions; changes trigger re-review
scenes.say: To recap. | Every model needs a named, accountable owner. | Independent validation provides effective challenge from people who didn’t build the model. | Risk tiers set the depth of validation, the level of approver and how often the model is reviewed. | And approvals carry conditions, with significant changes triggering review.

blocks.md:
### The model governance framework
Model governance applies the AI governance structures from Domain 2 to individual models across their lifecycle. Its foundations are:
- A **model inventory**, linked to the AI use-case inventory and AIBOMs, recording every model in use, including third-party and foundation models (Module 2.1).
- **Named ownership:** a business **model owner** accountable for use and outcomes, supported by technical owners.
- **Risk classification** that sets proportionate requirements.
- **Approval workflows** with defined evidence, approvers and conditions.
- **Ongoing review**, change management and retirement.

### Lessons from model risk management
Financial regulators have long required **model risk management**. The US guidance **SR 11-7** (2011) built it around sound development, **independent validation** and governance, centred on **effective challenge**: critical analysis by objective, informed people with the authority to make change happen. The UK PRA’s **SS1/23** (in force since 2024) sets model risk management principles for banks, explicitly including AI and machine learning models. These ideas transfer well to any organisation’s AI models.

### Classifying model risk
Typical criteria:
- **Impact** on people’s rights, safety, finances or opportunities.
- **Regulatory status**, for example an EU AI Act high-risk use case.
- **Autonomy and reversibility:** does the model decide or act on its own, and can outcomes be undone?
- **Scale:** how many people or decisions it affects.
- **Data sensitivity** and **complexity or opacity** of the model.
- **Exposure:** internal only, customer-facing, or open to the internet.

### Approval workflows
Each tier defines the required evidence (design documents, data approvals, validation results, security and privacy reviews), the approver, any **conditions** (limits on use, extra monitoring, human oversight) and the **review cycle**. Deviations go through the exception process (Module 2.6). Third-party and foundation models follow the same workflow, with validation adapted to the evidence available (vendor documentation, your own testing).

### Retirement
Retiring a model is a governed step too: notify users and dependent systems, revoke credentials and endpoints, archive documentation and evidence for the retention period, delete or retain artefacts according to policy, and update the inventory and AIBOM.

q.q: A team wants to deploy a vendor’s pre-trained model to screen job applicants. They argue it needs no internal approval because the vendor has already validated it. What is the BEST response?
o: Agree, because vendor validation replaces internal validation for pre-trained models
Tier it as high-risk and run the full approval workflow, adapting validation to the evidence available
Agree, provided the vendor’s contract includes an indemnity against any discrimination claims
Deploy it in production first, and complete the approval within six months if no problems arise
q.why: Hiring is a high-impact use, and accountability for using the model stays with the deployer. Vendor evidence informs validation but doesn’t replace the organisation’s own approval, testing and conditions. Indemnities transfer some cost, not accountability.

sections.title: Model cards and approved model registries

blocks.title: If it isn’t in the registry, it doesn’t ship

scenes.title: If it isn’t in the registry, it doesn’t ship
scenes.sub: Model documentation, model cards and approved model registries
scenes.say: Documentation turns a model from a black box into an accountable asset, and a registry makes sure only approved models reach production. | This video covers model cards and related documentation, and how an approved model registry works as a security control.

scenes.title: What a model card records

items.d: What it is for, and for whom
What it must not be used for
Broken down by group and condition

scenes.say: A model card is a short, structured summary of a model. | Intended use: what the model is for, and for whom. | Out-of-scope uses: what it must not be used for. | A training data summary: sources, time span and known gaps. | Evaluation results, broken down by relevant groups and conditions, not just one headline number. | Limitations and risks, including known failure modes. | And the owner, version and contact for questions or incidents.

scenes.title: The documentation set
scenes.say: Model cards sit within a wider documentation set. | A model card describes a trained model. A datasheet describes a dataset. A system card describes a whole AI system, including the model, its safeguards and how it is operated. | Model cards serve deployers, reviewers and users. Datasheets serve model builders and auditors. System cards serve users, regulators and sometimes the public. | They record intended use and limits; the origin and composition of data; and safeguards, testing and policies. For high-risk systems in the EU, technical documentation must cover all of this in more depth.

scenes.title: The registry as a deployment gate
scenes.say: An approved model registry is more than a catalogue. A candidate model arrives with its artefact, content hash and signature. | Its registry entry links the model card, lineage to data and training runs, and the evidence from testing. | Only an authorised approver can set its status to approved. | The deployment gate checks status and signature, and refuses anything that isn’t approved and unmodified. | So only registered, approved, verified models reach production. | And when a model is deprecated or retired, the registry blocks new deployments and flags existing ones for removal.

items: Model cards: intended use, limits, disaggregated results, owner
Datasheets for data; system cards for whole systems
The registry links artefacts, lineage, evidence and approvals
Deployment gates accept only approved, signed versions
scenes.say: To recap. | Model cards record intended and out-of-scope use, disaggregated results, limitations and the owner. | Datasheets document data, and system cards document whole AI systems. | The registry links each artefact to its lineage, evidence and approvals. | And deployment gates accept only approved, signed versions, which turns the registry into a security control.

blocks.md:
### Model documentation
- **Model cards** (introduced by Mitchell and colleagues in 2019) summarise a model’s intended use, out-of-scope uses, training data, evaluation results (disaggregated across groups and conditions), limitations, ethical considerations, version and owner.
- **Datasheets for datasets** document a dataset’s motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing, intended uses, distribution and maintenance (Module 3.1).
- **System cards** describe a complete AI system: model, safeguards, testing, deployment context and policies.
- For **high-risk systems under the EU AI Act**, providers must maintain technical documentation (Annex IV) covering the system’s description, development process, data, performance, risk management, human oversight, changes and monitoring; providers of general-purpose AI models have their own documentation duties. ISO/IEC 42001 also requires documentation of AI systems across their lifecycle.

Documentation should be **versioned with the model** and updated whenever the model, its data or its use changes. A model card that describes last year’s model is misleading.

### Approved model registries
A registry is the single source of truth for models and their status. It typically records:
- Each **model and version**, with artefact location, content hash and signature.
- **Status**: candidate, approved (with conditions), deprecated or retired.
- **Lineage**: datasets, code commit, training run and base model (Module 3.1).
- **Evidence**: validation results, security and privacy reviews, model card.
- **Approvals**: who approved, when, and under what conditions.
- **Deployments**: where each version runs, and its owner.
- Entries for **external and hosted models**, with pinned versions and vendor documentation.

### The registry as a security control
- **Deployment gating:** pipelines and serving platforms deploy only versions marked approved, with verified hashes and signatures (policy as code).
- **Separation of duties:** those who register models can’t approve them, and status changes are restricted and logged.
- **Immutability:** an approved version can’t be altered; any change creates a new version that needs approval.
- **Audit:** every registration, approval, deployment and retirement is logged.
- **Retirement:** deprecated or retired models are blocked from new deployments and flagged for removal.

blocks.title: Registry questions
blocks.md: When a question involves an unapproved or tampered model reaching production, the strongest control is usually **technical enforcement**: a deployment gate that accepts only **registry-approved, signed** versions. Policies, reminders and after-the-fact reports are weaker answers.

q.q: To meet a deadline, an engineer deploys a fine-tuned model straight from a training bucket to production, bypassing the registry. Which control MOST directly prevents this?
o: A policy statement reminding engineers that all production models must be registered first
A deployment gate that accepts only registry-approved models with valid signatures
A weekly report listing all models in production, reviewed by the AI governance lead
Training for engineers on why model registries matter for governance and audits
q.why: Technical enforcement at deployment stops unapproved artefacts reaching production. Policies and training rely on compliance, and weekly reports detect the problem only after it has happened.

blocks.title: From training run to production, safely

scenes.title: From training run to production, safely
scenes.sub: Validation, packaging, serving and credential management
scenes.say: The path from a training run to a production endpoint is a prime target: compromise it, and you control what every user receives. | This video covers securing that path, from validation gates and packaging, through serving, to the credentials the pipeline uses.

scenes.title: A secured deployment pipeline
scenes.say: Here is a secured deployment pipeline. A training run produces a candidate model. | A validation gate runs performance, safety, fairness and security tests, and scans the artefact for malicious content. | The model is packaged in a safe format with its dependencies, and signed, with a record of how it was built. | It is registered and approved. | Deployment to production needs approval, and uses dedicated credentials. | And it runs on hardened serving infrastructure: isolated, authenticated and rate-limited.

scenes.title: Validation gate checks
scenes.say: A validation gate should check six things. | Performance against the current production baseline. | Safety and robustness, using standard evaluation and red-team suites. | Fairness metrics for relevant groups. | Artefact scanning, for unsafe serialisation formats and embedded code. | Dependency and vulnerability scanning of the serving stack. | And provenance: the artefact’s hash matches the training run recorded in lineage.

scenes.title: Credentials in the pipeline

items.d: Never baked into images or packages

scenes.say: Pipelines run on credentials, and those credentials are high-value targets. | Use workload identity and short-lived tokens, not static keys stored in pipeline settings. | Separate credentials for each stage, so a compromised training job can’t deploy to production. | Require approval, ideally from two people, for production deployments of higher-risk models. | Inject secrets into serving at runtime from a vault, and never bake them into container images or model packages. | And monitor credential use, rotating on schedule and on any suspicion.

items: Gate releases on performance, safety, fairness and artefact scans
Package in safe formats; sign and record provenance
Serve on isolated, authenticated, rate-limited infrastructure
Short-lived, per-stage credentials; approvals for production
scenes.say: To recap. | Gate every release on performance, safety, fairness, artefact scanning and provenance. | Package models in safe formats, then sign them and record how they were built. | Serve them on isolated, authenticated, rate-limited infrastructure. | And use short-lived, per-stage credentials, with approvals for production deployments.

blocks.md:
### Pipeline stages and controls
| Stage | Key controls |
|---|---|
| **Train** | Isolated training environments; approved datasets pinned by hash (Module 3.3); recorded code commit, configuration and environment |
| **Validate** | Performance, safety, robustness and fairness test suites; artefact scanning for unsafe serialisation and embedded code; dependency scanning |
| **Package** | Safe weight formats (such as safetensors); minimal, scanned container images; SBOM and AIBOM generated |
| **Sign and attest** | Digital signatures on artefacts; provenance attestations describing how the model was built (for example, using SLSA-style provenance and Sigstore-based signing, as in the OpenSSF model signing specification) |
| **Register and approve** | Registry entry with evidence; approval by the right authority for the tier (Section 2) |
| **Deploy** | Deployment only of approved, verified versions; production approval; infrastructure as code; change records |
| **Serve** | Hardened inference servers; authentication and authorisation; rate limits and quotas; input size limits; network segmentation and restricted egress; no debug endpoints; prompt patching of the serving stack |

### Credential management
Pipeline credentials can deploy models, read training data and access production, so:
- Use **workload identity federation** and short-lived tokens instead of long-lived keys in pipeline settings.
- **Scope credentials per stage and environment**: training, validation, registry and production deployment each get their own.
- Require **approvals** for production deployments, with two-person review for higher-risk models.
- Inject **runtime secrets** (model API keys, database credentials) from a vault at start-up; never bake them into images, model packages or notebooks (Module 3.4).
- **Monitor** credential use and rotate regularly.

### Environment separation
Keep development, test and production separate, with production data kept out of development unless it is masked or synthetic. Promote **the same signed artefact** through environments, rather than rebuilding it at each stage, so what was tested is exactly what is deployed. Module 4.3 covers MLOps and LLMOps pipeline security in more depth.

q.q: A training job’s service account also has permission to deploy models to production. What is the MAIN risk?
o: Training will run more slowly, because the account must keep checking its deployment permissions
A compromised or faulty training job could push an unapproved model straight to production
The account’s credentials will expire more often, because they are used for two purposes
Auditors won’t be able to tell which data scientist trained each model in the registry
q.why: Combining training and deployment rights removes the separation that forces models through validation and approval. Per-stage credentials contain the impact of a compromised or faulty job.

sections.title: Sanitising inputs and outputs, updates and rollback

blocks.title: Clean in, clean out, and a way back

scenes.title: Clean in, clean out, and a way back
scenes.say: A deployed model is only as safe as what goes into it and what comes out of it, and every update is a chance to break both. | This video covers sanitising inputs and outputs, releasing updates safely, and rolling back quickly when an update goes wrong.

scenes.title: Sanitise in both directions
rows: Keep bad input from the model
Keep unsafe output from users and systems
scenes.say: Sanitisation works in both directions. | On the input side, the goal is to stop harmful or malformed content reaching the model. On the output side, it is to stop unsafe output reaching users or downstream systems. | Input controls include validation, size limits, normalisation and screening for injection attempts. Output controls include encoding, schema validation, data loss prevention and moderation. | Input controls target prompt injection and oversized or hidden content. Output controls target script and command injection, data leakage and harmful content. | For example: strip hidden text from uploaded documents on the way in, and encode the model’s reply before a web page displays it.

scenes.title: Treat model output as untrusted

items.d: No eval, no raw shell or SQL

scenes.say: The OWASP Top 10 for large language model applications lists improper output handling as a major risk. The fix starts with a mindset: treat model output exactly like untrusted user input. | Encode it for wherever it is going: HTML, SQL, a shell, or rendered Markdown. | Validate structured output against a schema, with allowed fields and values. | Never pass output straight into code execution, a shell or a database query. | Give the tools and systems that act on output only the rights they need. | And inspect replies with data loss prevention and moderation before they reach people.

scenes.title: Releasing an update safely
scenes.say: Here is a safe release path for a new model version, after it has been approved. | First, offline evaluation: regression tests against the current version, plus the safety, security and fairness suites. | Next, shadow mode: the new version receives a copy of real traffic, but its answers are only compared, never shown to users. | Then a canary release to a small percentage of users, with close monitoring. | If the signals stay healthy, the rollout widens step by step. | And if they don’t, the team rolls back to the previous approved version straight away, using triggers and authority agreed in advance.

scenes.title: What a rollback must restore
scenes.say: A rollback has to restore the whole system, not just the weights. Keep a complete, tested bundle for the previous version. | The model version itself, signed and still held in the registry. | The system prompt and generation settings it was tested with. | The guardrail configuration: filters, policies and thresholds. | For retrieval systems, the index and the embedding model that built it. | The serving image and its dependencies. | And the feature pipeline and data schemas the model expects.

items: Sanitise inputs, and treat outputs as untrusted
Encode for the destination; never execute output
Release through evaluation, shadow and canary stages
Pre-agree rollback triggers; restore the full bundle
scenes.say: To recap. | Sanitise what goes in, and treat what comes out as untrusted. | Encode output for its destination, validate its structure, and never execute it directly. | Release updates through offline evaluation, shadow mode and canary stages. | And agree rollback triggers and authority in advance, so you can restore the complete previous bundle within minutes.

blocks.md:
### Input sanitisation
Inputs include user prompts, uploaded files, retrieved documents, tool results and API parameters. Controls:
- **Validation:** type, length, format and allowed values for structured fields; reject or truncate oversized inputs (token and file size limits also protect availability, Module 3.6).
- **Normalisation:** standardise Unicode (for example with NFKC), remove invisible and zero-width characters, and map look-alike characters from other alphabets, all of which can hide instructions or evade filters.
- **File sanitisation:** content disarm and reconstruction (CDR) rebuilds documents without macros, scripts, hidden text or metadata; convert formats where possible (for example, to plain text) before the model sees them.
- **Screening:** classifiers that detect likely prompt injection or abuse, and DLP that redacts sensitive data before external models (Module 3.4).
- **Separation:** mark retrieved and uploaded content as untrusted data, kept apart from instructions.

No input filter reliably stops every prompt injection, so input controls are one layer. **Output handling and least privilege** must assume that some malicious input gets through.

### Output sanitisation
The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) lists **LLM05: Improper Output Handling**: passing model output to other components without validation, which can lead to cross-site scripting, server-side request forgery, privilege escalation or remote code execution. Controls:
- **Context-aware encoding:** HTML-encode text before inserting it into a page, or render it as plain text; use a content security policy as a backstop.
- **Restricted rendering:** limit what rendered Markdown can do, for example by blocking images from external domains, which can be used to send data out through the image address.
- **Schema validation** for structured output, rejecting unexpected fields or values.
- **Parameterised queries** when output feeds a database; **no direct execution** of generated code or commands, except in a sandbox built for it.
- **Allow-lists** for URLs, tools and actions; **human approval** for high-impact actions.
- **DLP and moderation** on outputs, to catch leaked secrets, personal data and harmful content.

Module 4.4 covers guardrail architecture and context boundary validation in more depth.

### Updating models safely
Updates come in many forms: retrained or fine-tuned versions, a provider’s new base model, system prompt and configuration changes, guardrail changes, retrieval index rebuilds and serving stack patches. Each goes through **change management**, scaled to the risk tier (Section 1): re-run the evaluation suites, update the registry and model card, and get the approval the tier requires.
- **Pin versions** of hosted models (for example, a dated model version rather than a "latest" alias), so the provider can’t change behaviour without your testing. Track deprecation notices and plan migrations early.
- **Release strategies:** *shadow mode* (mirror traffic, compare outputs, serve nothing), *canary* (a small share of users first), *blue/green* (two production environments, switching traffic between them for instant rollback) and *feature flags* (turn a capability on or off without redeploying).

### Rollback procedures
- **Define triggers in advance:** error rates, safety or policy violations, fairness gaps, drift alerts, security incidents or user complaints above a threshold.
- **Pre-authorise** who can roll back, such as the on-call engineer or model owner, so rollback doesn’t wait for a committee.
- **Keep the previous version deployable:** retained in the registry, with capacity to run it, and the full bundle (model, prompts, settings, guardrails, index, serving image, feature pipeline).
- **Test rollback** regularly, as you would disaster recovery.
- **Record and learn:** log the rollback in the registry and incident record, find the root cause, and re-approve before re-releasing.
- **Have a kill switch:** a way to disable the AI feature entirely and fall back to a non-AI process if no safe version is available (Module 5.7 covers circuit breakers and kill switches in recovery).

Rollback has limits. It can’t recall data that has already leaked, emails already sent or actions an agent has already taken, and a model that learned continuously from poisoned feedback must be restored from a checkpoint taken before the poisoning began.

blocks.title: Spotting the best answer
blocks.md: For output risks, look for **controls outside the model**: encoding, schema validation, sandboxing and least privilege. Instructions in the system prompt ("never output HTML") are weak, because the model can be manipulated. For bad releases, the best answer is usually a **pre-planned rollback to the last approved version**, followed by root-cause analysis, rather than a rushed fix in production.

q.q: A support chatbot’s replies are inserted into the agent console as HTML. A tester shows that a crafted customer message makes the bot return markup that runs script in the agent’s browser. What is the BEST fix?
o: Tell the model in its system prompt never to produce HTML or script in replies
Encode the bot’s output for the HTML context before display, backed by a content security policy
Move to a larger model, which is less likely to follow instructions hidden in messages
Block any customer message that contains the word “script” or angle brackets
q.why: Model output must be handled as untrusted input: context-aware encoding stops it running as code, and a content security policy adds defence in depth. Prompt instructions and bigger models can still be manipulated, and keyword blocking is easily evaded.

sections.title: Security lifecycle monitoring: drift, bias and anomalies

scenes.title: Is the model still behaving?
scenes.sub: Drift, bias tracking and anomaly detection
scenes.say: Approval is a snapshot of a model on one day. Production is everything that happens afterwards: the world changes, users change, and attackers start probing. | This video covers monitoring across the lifecycle: drift, bias tracking and anomaly detection, and how monitoring feeds back into governance.

scenes.title: What to monitor in production

items.d: Inputs move away from training data

scenes.say: Monitoring covers six areas. | Data drift: inputs moving away from what the model was trained on. Module 1.3 covers the drift types and the statistics used to measure them. | Performance, measured against real outcomes once they are known, which can take weeks or months. | Fairness: outcomes and error rates for each relevant group. | Output behaviour, such as refusal rates, toxicity and, for generative systems, how well answers are grounded in sources. | Security signals: probing, extraction attempts and abuse. | And operations: latency, errors and cost, where sudden changes can also signal an attack.

scenes.title: Bias can drift too
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative gap in approval rates between two groups, in percentage points
scenes.say: Fairness isn’t fixed at approval. In this illustrative chart, the gap in approval rates between two groups starts small, then widens as the applicant population and economic conditions change. | When the model was approved, its owner set a tolerance of four percentage points, recorded in the monitoring plan. | In month six the gap crosses the tolerance and an alert goes to the owner. The first job is to find out why: has the population shifted, has a data pipeline broken, or has the model degraded for one group?

scenes.title: Anomalies worth an alert
scenes.say: Security monitoring looks for anomalies against a baseline. | A spike in query volume from one account or API key can signal model extraction or abuse. | Many systematic, near-duplicate queries suggest someone probing the model’s decision boundaries. | Inputs far from the training distribution may be adversarial, or a sign the model is being used outside its approved scope. | Unusual outputs, such as leaked personal data, sudden changes in refusals, or repeated policy violations, need investigation. | And agents that call new tools, touch unfamiliar data or send data to new destinations should raise an alert.

scenes.title: Monitoring feeds governance
scenes.say: Monitoring only matters if it changes decisions. It starts at approval, with a monitoring plan that names the metrics, the thresholds and the owner. | Monitoring then runs continuously across drift, fairness, security and operations. | When a threshold is crossed, an alert fires. | It goes to the model owner, who leads triage to find the cause. | The response might be retraining, recalibrating, restricting use or rolling back. | And governance records catch up: the registry, the risk record and the model card are updated, and a material change goes back through validation and approval.

items: Monitor drift, performance, fairness, behaviour, security and operations
Set metrics, thresholds and owners at approval
Baseline normal use; alert on anomalies such as probing
Feed results into the registry, risk records and re-approval
scenes.say: To recap. | Monitor drift, performance, fairness, output behaviour, security signals and operations. | Set the metrics, thresholds and owner at approval, in a monitoring plan. | Baseline normal use, and alert on anomalies such as volume spikes and systematic probing. | And feed what you find back into the registry, the risk records and, when needed, re-approval.

blocks.md:
### Monitoring across the lifecycle
Monitoring starts at approval: the **monitoring plan** (part of the approval record and model card) names the metrics, thresholds, review frequency and accountable owner. Module 1.3 explains the drift types (data, concept, label) and measures such as the population stability index.

| Area | Example signals |
|---|---|
| **Data drift** | Input distribution shifts, new categories, changes in prompt topics or languages, embedding drift |
| **Performance** | Accuracy, precision and recall once outcomes arrive; proxy measures while labels are delayed |
| **Fairness** | Selection rates and error rates (false positives, false negatives) by group, against tolerances |
| **Output behaviour** | Refusal rates, toxicity, hallucination or groundedness scores on sampled outputs, output length |
| **Security** | Query volume and patterns per identity, out-of-distribution inputs, prompt injection detections, data leakage in outputs, agent tool use |
| **Operations** | Latency, error rates, token use and cost; sudden spikes can indicate abuse or denial of service |

### Bias tracking
- Define the **groups and fairness metrics** at approval, with **tolerances** (for example, a maximum gap in approval rates or in false negative rates).
- Track them on a schedule that fits the risk, and investigate when tolerances are breached. Possible causes include population change, broken pipelines, proxy variables and feedback loops.
- Data about protected characteristics is often sensitive or missing. Use privacy-preserving approaches, such as aggregate analysis in a restricted environment, with legal advice on what may be collected.
- For high-risk systems, the EU AI Act requires providers to run a **post-market monitoring system** (Article 72) and deployers to monitor operation according to the instructions for use (Article 26). ISO/IEC 42001 (Clause 9, performance evaluation) and the NIST AI RMF *Measure* and *Manage* functions expect the same continuous measurement.

### Anomaly detection
- **Baseline** normal behaviour per user, API key, application and agent, then alert on deviations: volume spikes, unusual hours, high query diversity or systematic variation (signs of extraction or boundary probing; Module 3.6).
- **Out-of-distribution detection:** flag inputs whose features or embeddings are far from the training data.
- **Output monitors:** detect personal data, secrets, policy violations and canary strings planted to reveal leakage of training data or system prompts.
- **Agent monitoring:** new tools, unusual data volumes, new destinations or privilege changes.
- Send AI detections to the **security operations centre** alongside other telemetry, with runbooks for AI incidents (Modules 5.2 and 5.3).

### Closing the loop
Alerts route to the **model owner**. Responses include retraining or recalibrating, tightening guardrails, restricting use, rolling back (Section 4) or retiring the model. Results update the **registry, risk register and model card**. A material change in behaviour, data or use triggers **revalidation and re-approval**, and every model gets a periodic review whose frequency depends on its risk tier.

q.q: A credit model was approved with a 2-point gap in approval rates between two groups and a 4-point tolerance. Monitoring now shows a gap of 4.6 points. What should happen FIRST?
o: Retrain the model straight away on the most recent applications, then redeploy it
The model owner investigates the cause under the monitoring plan and decides on interim steps
Raise the tolerance to 5 points, because the applicant population has clearly changed since approval
Stop collecting group data, so that the gap can no longer be measured or disclosed
q.why: A breached tolerance triggers the agreed response: the accountable owner investigates the cause and decides on interim measures. Retraining without a diagnosis may repeat the problem, moving the threshold hides it, and dropping measurement removes the control.

scenes.title: Record everything, expose nothing
scenes.sub: Privacy-preserving audit trails for AI data events
scenes.say: AI systems need audit trails: to investigate incidents, prove compliance and reconstruct how a decision was made. | But the prompts and outputs most worth logging are often the most sensitive data you hold. This video covers how to record AI data events without creating a new privacy problem.

scenes.title: AI data events to record
scenes.say: Start by deciding which events matter. | Data access: which datasets were read, and which documents retrieval returned. | Training and fine-tuning: each run, the data versions it used, and who launched it. | Model changes: registrations, approvals, deployments and rollbacks. | Inference: who called which model version, when, what was decided, and which policies fired. | Agent actions: every tool call, and the data each one touched. | And data subject events: consent changes, access and erasure requests, and unlearning.

scenes.title: Finding the balance
rows: A new trove of sensitive data
scenes.say: Logging is a balance. | Log too little, and you can’t reconstruct an incident. Log too much, and the evidence is buried in noise. | Too little, and you can’t show the traceability that regulators expect. Too much, and you break data minimisation and storage limits. | Logging too little creates little privacy risk, but logging everything creates a new store of highly sensitive data. | And if that store is breached, every prompt and output in it is exposed.

scenes.title: A privacy-preserving logging design
scenes.say: Here is one design that keeps both accountability and privacy. The AI application emits events as it works. | Metadata goes to the main event log: who, when, which model version, which policies fired, and a keyed hash of the content, with user identifiers pseudonymised. | Content, meaning prompts and outputs, goes only where it is needed, into a separate vault: redacted, encrypted with its own keys, and kept for a short time. | The event log is written to tamper-evident storage: append-only, with each entry chained to the hash of the one before. | Reading the content vault needs break-glass access: approved, tied to a stated purpose such as an investigation, and itself logged. | And everything follows a retention schedule, with deletion carried out automatically.

scenes.title: Privacy techniques for audit logs

items.d: Log what a defined purpose needs

scenes.say: Five techniques do most of the work. | Minimise: log what a defined purpose needs, and no more. | Pseudonymise user identifiers with keyed hashes, holding the key separately, so re-identification needs a controlled step. | Redact personal data and secrets from prompts and outputs before they are stored, using the same data loss prevention as the gateway. | Encrypt logs with their own keys and access roles, separate from the systems they record. | And keep logs for as long as law and purpose require, then delete them automatically.

items: Decide which AI data events must be recorded, and why
Keep metadata and content apart; protect content most
Make logs tamper-evident; control and log access to them
Minimise, pseudonymise, redact, encrypt, and delete on schedule
scenes.say: To recap. | Decide which AI data events must be recorded, and for what purpose. | Keep metadata and content apart, and protect the content most strongly. | Make logs tamper-evident, and control and log every access to them. | And minimise, pseudonymise, redact, encrypt, and delete on schedule.

blocks.md:
### Why AI audit trails matter
Audit trails let you investigate incidents (what data did the agent access, and which model version answered?), demonstrate compliance, support people’s rights (what was decided about me, and how?) and prove that deletion and unlearning requests were carried out.

### Requirements to know
| Source | What it requires |
|---|---|
| **EU AI Act, Article 12** | High-risk AI systems must technically allow **automatic recording of events (logs)** over their lifetime, to support traceability, post-market monitoring and identification of risks |
| **EU AI Act, Articles 19 and 26(6)** | Providers and deployers keep the logs under their control for a period appropriate to the purpose, **at least six months**, unless other law (such as data protection law) provides otherwise |
| **GDPR** | Logs containing personal data are personal data: data minimisation, storage limitation, security (Article 32), and they fall within access and erasure requests |
| **HIPAA Security Rule** | **Audit controls** (45 CFR 164.312(b)): mechanisms to record and examine activity in systems containing ePHI |
| **PCI DSS v4.0, Requirement 10** | Log and monitor all access to cardholder data; keep audit logs for **at least 12 months**, with the last 3 months immediately available |
| **ISO/IEC 42001** | Annex A control on recording event logs for AI systems, at least while the system is in use |

### Designing privacy-preserving audit trails
- **Separate metadata from content.** The main event log records who, what, when, which model version, which data sources and which policies fired. Prompts and outputs go to a separate, more restricted store, only where a defined purpose needs them.
- **Link without exposing.** Store a **keyed hash** of each prompt and output in the event log. Investigators can then prove what was said by matching retained content to its hash, without the main log holding the text. The hash must be keyed, because short or predictable text can otherwise be guessed and confirmed.
- **Pseudonymise** user identifiers with keyed hashing (Module 3.2), with the key held by a separate team. Pseudonymised data is still personal data under the GDPR.
- **Redact or tokenise** personal data and secrets before storage, using the gateway’s DLP (Module 3.4).
- **Encrypt** with dedicated keys. Per-user or per-period keys make deletion practical through **crypto-shredding**, which helps with erasure requests and retention limits.
- **Control access.** Grant least privilege, require **break-glass** approval and a stated purpose to read content, and log every access to the logs themselves.
- **Make logs tamper-evident.** Use write-once (WORM) storage, **hash chaining** (each entry includes the hash of the previous one) or Merkle trees, signed checkpoints and trusted timestamps, with log administration separated from the systems being logged.
- **Retain deliberately.** Set periods from legal minimums and purpose, delete automatically, and use a formal **legal hold** to suspend deletion when litigation or an investigation requires it.
- **Cover suppliers.** Model providers may keep your prompts for abuse monitoring. Check retention terms and zero-data-retention options in the contract (Modules 2.4 and 2.5).

For analysis across many users, such as usage trends or abuse patterns, prefer aggregated statistics, and consider differential privacy for metrics shared widely. Module 5.2 covers security telemetry pipelines, log integrity and evidence handling in operations.

blocks.title: Audit trail questions
blocks.md: Expect answers to balance **accountability with privacy**. "Log nothing" fails traceability, and "log every prompt forever in the central SIEM" fails minimisation and security. The best answer usually **records event metadata broadly, keeps content selectively in a protected store, makes logs tamper-evident and limits retention**.

q.q: A team proposes logging every full prompt and response indefinitely in the central SIEM, so that investigators always have complete records. What is the BEST response?
o: Approve it, because complete and permanent records always give investigators the best evidence
Log metadata centrally; keep redacted content in a separate encrypted store with access and retention limits
Stop logging AI interactions altogether, because prompts are too sensitive to store anywhere
Log only the prompts, because responses are generated by the model and so contain no personal data
q.why: Metadata in the central log supports investigations, while redacted content in a separate, encrypted, access-controlled store with retention limits respects minimisation and security. Permanent full logging creates a sensitive trove; logging nothing loses traceability; outputs can contain personal data too.

quiz.q: Who should be accountable for a production model’s use and outcomes?
o: The data scientist who trained the most recent version of the model
A named model owner, usually in the business area that relies on it
The vendor that supplied the base model the system was built on
The security team, because it reviews every model before deployment
quiz.why: Accountability sits with a named business owner, supported by technical owners. Developers, vendors and security teams contribute, but they don’t own the model’s use and outcomes.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN purpose of classifying models into risk tiers?
o: To decide which models can skip documentation and approval altogether
To scale validation, approval and monitoring to each model’s potential impact
To rank data science teams by the commercial value of the models they build
To choose which cloud provider should host each model once it reaches production
quiz.why: Risk tiers make governance proportionate: higher-impact models get deeper validation, more senior approval and closer monitoring. Even low-tier models still need basic records.

quiz.q: Which content is MOST essential in a model card?
o: The full training code and every hyperparameter tried during model development
Intended and out-of-scope uses, results across groups, and known limitations
The names and contact details of everyone who labelled the training data
Marketing claims comparing the model’s accuracy with competing products
quiz.why: A model card tells users and reviewers what a model is for, how it performs across groups and conditions, and where it shouldn’t be used. Code, personal details and marketing claims don’t belong there.

quiz.q: How does an approved model registry act as a security control?
o: It stores model weights in encrypted form, so that nobody can steal them
Deployment pipelines accept only registry-approved versions with valid signatures
It retrains models automatically whenever their measured performance starts to decline
It lets any engineer update an approved version in place, keeping one record
quiz.why: Gating deployment on approval status and verified signatures stops unapproved or tampered models reaching production. Approved versions should be immutable, so changes create new versions.

quiz.q: Why should the same signed artefact be promoted through test and production, rather than rebuilt at each stage?
o: Rebuilding the model at every stage would use more storage space in the registry
It guarantees that exactly what was tested is what is deployed in production
Signed artefacts load faster on inference servers than freshly rebuilt ones do
Regulators forbid rebuilding a model once its first version has been signed
quiz.why: Promoting one signed artefact preserves integrity: any rebuild could introduce differences, accidental or malicious, that testing never saw.

quiz.q: Where should a model-serving container get its database credentials?
o: From environment variables written into the container image when it is built
From a secrets vault at start-up, using the workload’s own cloud identity
From a configuration file stored alongside the model weights in the registry
From the system prompt, so the model can connect whenever it needs data
quiz.why: Runtime injection from a vault, authenticated by workload identity, keeps secrets out of images, packages and prompts, where they can be extracted or copied.

quiz.q: Which risk does OWASP call improper output handling in LLM applications?
o: Users receiving answers that are too long or detailed for their needs
Model output passed to other components without validation or encoding
Models refusing too many legitimate requests because filters are too strict
Replies arriving slowly because the serving cluster is badly overloaded
quiz.why: LLM05: Improper Output Handling covers output that reaches browsers, databases, shells or tools without validation, leading to injection, privilege escalation or code execution.

quiz.q: What should a rollback plan for an LLM application restore?
o: Only the model weights, because nothing else changes during an update
The full tested bundle: model, prompts, settings, guardrails and index
Only the system prompt, because it is the easiest component to change
Only the guardrail filters, because that is where most failures occur
quiz.why: Behaviour depends on the whole system. Restoring only one component can leave an untested combination running in production.

quiz.q: Why is model performance often hard to measure directly in production?
o: Production systems can’t record the predictions that a model makes
True outcomes, such as defaults or fraud, may arrive weeks or months later
Performance metrics are meaningful only during the training and testing phases
Monitoring tools can’t measure the accuracy of classification models
quiz.why: Ground truth is often delayed, so teams watch proxies such as data drift and prediction drift until real outcomes arrive.

quiz.q: Overnight, one account sends tens of thousands of systematically varied queries to a model’s API. What does this MOST likely indicate?
o: A routine batch job, which should be excluded from monitoring
An attempt to extract the model or probe its decision boundaries
Concept drift caused by a change in the customer population
A fairness problem that affects one group of users in particular
quiz.why: High-volume, systematic querying from one identity is a classic sign of extraction or boundary probing. It needs investigation and rate limiting (Module 3.6).

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, what record-keeping must high-risk AI systems support?
o: Manual logging by operators, reviewed by the provider once a year
Automatic recording of events (logs) over the system’s lifetime
Storage of every prompt and output for at least ten years
Logging that starts only once an incident has been reported
quiz.why: Article 12 requires high-risk systems to technically allow automatic event logging throughout their lifetime. Providers and deployers keep the logs for at least six months, unless other law provides otherwise.

quiz.q: Why should a hash of prompt content in an audit log be keyed, for example with an HMAC?
o: Keyed hashes are shorter, which reduces the cost of storing logs
Without a key, short or predictable content could be guessed and confirmed
Keyed hashes can be reversed to recover the original prompt whenever it is needed
Regulations require every hash in a log to use one public key
quiz.why: An unkeyed hash of predictable text can be brute-forced by hashing likely inputs. A secret key prevents this, while still letting authorised investigators match retained content to the log.

exam.q: A bank’s data science team has deployed 40 models over three years. An internal audit finds that 12 have no identified owner, and several are used for decisions their documentation doesn’t mention. What should the CISO recommend FIRST?
o: Retire all 12 unowned models immediately, whatever disruption that causes to the business
Build a model inventory with named owners and risk tiers, then review each model’s use against its approval
Require model cards for all 40 models before the team is allowed to make any further deployments
Commission an external penetration test of the 12 unowned models to find out whether they are vulnerable
exam.why: Governance starts with knowing what exists and who is accountable. An inventory with owners and risk tiers lets the bank prioritise reviews of models used beyond their approval. Retiring everything is disproportionate, and documentation and testing follow ownership and classification.

exam.q: A vendor’s model card says the model was evaluated only on English-language data and must not be used for medical advice. A business unit wants to use it to answer patients’ questions in Spanish. What is the BEST course of action?
o: Proceed, because a vendor’s model card is guidance rather than a contractual restriction
Treat it as an out-of-scope use: assess the risk, test for the actual use, and get approval first
Translate the patients’ questions into English first, which keeps the use within the card’s scope
Add a disclaimer to every answer stating that it isn’t medical advice, and then deploy it
exam.why: The use falls outside the documented scope on two counts, language and medical advice, so it needs its own risk assessment, testing for the real use and approval. Translation and disclaimers don’t make an out-of-scope use safe.

exam.q: An auditor finds that the pipeline deploying models to production authenticates with one long-lived cloud access key, stored in the pipeline settings and shared by every stage. What is the BEST remediation?
o: Rotate the access key every 90 days, and restrict who can view the pipeline settings
Use short-lived workload identity credentials scoped to each stage, with approval for production
Encrypt the access key within the pipeline settings, using the pipeline tool’s built-in secret masking
Move the access key into the model package, so that it travels with the approved artefact
exam.why: Workload identity removes long-lived secrets, per-stage scoping stops a compromised stage reaching production, and approvals add a human check. Rotation and masking still leave one powerful shared key, and embedding keys in packages spreads them further.

exam.q: A retailer releases a new version of its product-description LLM. Within an hour of the full release, customers report offensive descriptions; the previous version had no such problem. What should the team do FIRST?
o: Patch the system prompt in production with stricter instructions, and monitor the results closely
Roll back to the previous approved bundle under the pre-agreed procedure, then investigate fully
Take the whole website offline until the base model’s vendor explains the change in behaviour
Add the reported phrases to the output blocklist, and keep the new version running meanwhile
exam.why: A pre-planned rollback quickly restores a known-good state and limits harm; root-cause analysis and re-approval follow. Hot-patching prompts or blocklists treats symptoms and may miss other failures, and taking the site offline is disproportionate when a safe version exists.

exam.q: An AI agent summarises incoming supplier emails and can create purchase orders through an API. A red team shows that an email containing hidden instructions can make the agent raise an order. Which control BEST limits the impact?
o: A stronger system prompt that tells the agent to ignore any instructions it finds inside supplier emails
Treat the agent’s proposed actions as untrusted: validate them, and require human approval for orders
Scan all incoming email with antivirus software before the agent is allowed to read it
Train procurement staff to report suspicious supplier emails promptly to the security team
exam.why: Prompt injection can’t be reliably filtered, so impact must be limited outside the model: validating proposed actions and requiring human approval for orders stops a manipulated agent acting alone. Prompt instructions can be overridden, and antivirus doesn’t detect instructions written in natural language.

exam.q: Monitoring shows that a hiring model’s false negative rate for older applicants has doubled in six months, breaching its tolerance. The team retrains the model on recent data, and offline tests show the gap has closed. What should happen BEFORE the retrained model replaces the current one?
o: Deploy it straight away, because the offline tests show the gap has now closed
Validate and approve it as a new version for its tier, and update the registry, risk record and model card
Delete the monitoring data from the breach period, to limit the organisation’s legal exposure
Lower the fairness tolerance for the next six months to compensate for the breach period
exam.why: A retrained model is a material change, so it needs the validation and approval its tier requires, and governance records must capture the breach, its cause and the fix. Deleting evidence is improper, and adjusting tolerances doesn’t address the cause.

exam.q: A hospital’s clinical summarisation assistant must keep audit records for incident investigations. The privacy officer worries that the logs will become a new store of patient data. Which design BEST meets both needs?
o: Store full prompts and outputs in the general application log, where investigators can search them easily
Log metadata with pseudonymous IDs in tamper-evident storage; keep redacted content in a restricted vault
Log nothing about how the assistant is used, so that no patient information can ever leak from logs
Keep complete logs only on clinicians’ own devices, where device encryption protects them from theft
exam.why: Separating pseudonymised metadata (in tamper-evident storage) from redacted content (in a restricted vault with break-glass access and retention limits) supports investigations while minimising exposure. Full logs in a general store create a sensitive trove, no logs lose traceability, and device-held logs are neither controlled nor reliable.
